summary: A warned pestilence kills Egyptian livestock in the field while Israel’s animals are spared; ashes then produce boils that prevent even the magicians from standing before Moses. Before a destructive hailstorm, Egyptians are told to shelter people and animals, yet those left outside die; Pharaoh admits sin, asks for relief, and hardens his heart again when the storm stops.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows warnings that allow some Egyptians to protect their households even within a severe judgment. It also puts Pharaoh’s confession beside his repeated refusal and records both divine and human hardening language.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Pharaoh’s court, Egyptian fields and livestock, and Goshen during successive pestilence, boils, and hail.
context.literaryForm: Three escalating plague episodes with announced timing, exemptions, a shelter warning, confession, intercession, and reversal.

before.text: Pharaoh has hardened his heart after the flies are removed. The next demand warns of a pestilence against Egyptian livestock.

here.text: Livestock disease, boils, and hail affect Egypt; the final warning gives people an opportunity to shelter those in the field.

after.text: The locust warning focuses on what survived the hail, and Pharaoh’s own servants now urge him to release at least some of the people.

outline.heading: Pestilence and a distinction
outline.note: A set-time disease strikes Egyptian livestock but not Israel’s, and Pharaoh remains stubborn.

outline.heading: Ashes and boils
outline.note: People, animals, and magicians are affected; Yahweh hardens Pharaoh’s heart.

outline.heading: Hail warning and a chance for shelter
outline.note: Moses announces an exceptional storm, and some of Pharaoh’s servants move people and animals inside.

outline.heading: Hail and destruction
outline.note: Thunder, lightning, and hail strike the field while Goshen is spared.

outline.heading: Confession, intercession, and renewed refusal
outline.note: Pharaoh asks for prayer; after the storm ends he and his servants harden their hearts.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken to Moses.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s explicit report that Yahweh hardens Pharaoh’s heart.

keyVerses.text: Those who feared Yahweh’s word among the servants of Pharaoh made their servants and their livestock flee into the houses.
keyVerses.why: Some Egyptians respond to the warning by sheltering their servants and livestock.

keyVerses.text: When Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunders had ceased, he sinned yet more, and hardened his heart, he and his servants.
keyVerses.why: Pharaoh and his servants harden their hearts again after relief from the hail.

questions.question: How can later livestock be sheltered if “all” Egyptian livestock died earlier?
questions.answer: The warning specifies livestock in the field, which may limit its scope, while verse 6 says “all the livestock of Egypt died.” Later the hail warning addresses livestock in the field again. The text gives these statements without explaining the apparent tension or narrating replacement herds.

questions.question: How is Israel distinguished in the livestock plague?
questions.answer: The warning says Israel’s animals will not die, and Pharaoh checks the result before continuing to refuse release. This distinction is narrated as part of the sign, not as evidence that Egyptian herders had caused the king’s decision.

questions.question: What are “boils” in this episode?
questions.answer: They are painful eruptions or blisters that break out on people and animals after ashes are thrown toward the sky. The text does not identify a modern disease, and it says even the magicians cannot stand before Moses because they are affected.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart?
questions.answer: After the boils the narrator says Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart. After the hail ceases it says Pharaoh sinned again and hardened his heart along with his servants; the text keeps both descriptions in the sequence.

questions.question: What can Egyptians do before the hail arrives?
questions.answer: The warning tells them to bring servants and livestock out of the field into shelter. Some of Pharaoh’s servants fear the word and do so, while others leave them outside where the storm will strike.

questions.question: Who dies or loses resources in the hail?
questions.answer: The storm strikes people and animals left in the field, plants, and trees, while Goshen is exempt. The account therefore includes losses borne by households and workers beyond Pharaoh, even though some heed the warning.

questions.question: Does Pharaoh’s admission of sin lead to release?
questions.answer: He says Yahweh is righteous and asks Moses to pray, promising to let Israel go. Once the thunder, hail, and rain stop, he hardens his heart and does not release the people.

questions.question: Why mention flax, barley, wheat, and spelt?
questions.answer: The text says flax and barley are damaged because of their growth stage, while wheat and spelt have not yet grown up and remain. This detail prepares the later locusts to consume what the hail left behind.

glossary.def: The severe affliction announced against Egyptian livestock in the field.
The bodily eruptions that affect Egyptians, animals, and the court magicians.
A crop not struck with the earlier-grown flax and barley in the hail account.
